newsitem.title: UK: Cry for change puts UK's Labour ahead-Reuters poll.
newsitem.headline: Cry for change puts UK's Labour ahead-Reuters poll.

text.p: The first major opinion poll of Britain's election campaign on Tuesday put the opposition Labour party 25 points ahead of the Conservatives with 54 percent of the vote despite Prime Minister John Major's confidence that he would win.

An exclusive poll by NOP for Reuters underlined the chances of an overwhelming victory for Tony Blair's Labour party on May 1, with evidence of strong popular sentiment that it was time for a change after 18 years of Conservative government.

The survey of 1,065 people around Britain conducted on March 14, before Monday's announcement of the election date, showed Labour pulling nine points ahead of the Conservatives even in its rating on managing the economy.

NOP's adjusted figures, taking into account the likely votes of people who did not express a party preference, showed Labour up four points to 54 percent since the organisation's first poll for Reuters on February 21.
Support for the Conservatives slipped one percentage point to 29 percent, while the Liberal Democrats lost three points to 11 percent.

The survey confirmed Labour's striking lead in recent opinion polls which, under Britain's first-past-the-post electoral system, would give it an enormous majority in parliament if translated into votes.

The poll found little evidence that support for the main parties was weak among those who had a preference; some 63 percent said they were "not at all likely" to change their mind about which party they would vote for between now and election day.
Another 63 percent predicted Labour would win, regardless of how they voted personally.
Asked to choose the single main reason for their decision on how to vote, more than a quarter of respondents -- 26 percent -- said it was time for a change.

More than a third of these were in the category of skilled manual workers whom former prime minister Margaret Thatcher won over to the Conservative cause in the 1980s with her policies of selling council homes and extending share ownership.

The poll showed that the Conservatives were not being rewarded for improvements in the economy since the recession of the early 1990s, with 35 percent of people interviewed saying they trusted Labour most to manage the economy, compared to 26 percent for the Conservatives.

Some 39 percent thought they would be better off under Labour, taking into account income, benefits and pensions against expenditure and taxes. Twenty-six percent thought the Conservatives would do more for their personal finances.
Major did not score badly with voters asked to rate his performance as prime minister, with 31 percent saying he had done "fairly well" against 20 percent who said he had performed "very badly".
But, underlining the yearning for a change, Blair was given a thumbs-up from 41 percent who thought he had done "fairly well" as opposition leader.

Less than 20 percent mentioned taxation, unemployment or inflation as major influences on their vote compared to around a third who said education and the state health system -- key planks in Labour's platform -- were most important.
Three percent said they would vote for Scottish and Welsh nationalists, one percent for the Referendum Party opposed to European integration, and two percent for other minor parties.
